conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. Johnson. I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you’ve been feeling confused and unwell. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… I’ve been foggy all day. Took Percocet for my arm pain—fell a few days ago, broke my humerus. Was taking one, then two every four hours. Last night I took them closer together. Felt drowsy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And this morning, you took more and your wife noticed you weren’t yourself?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Took two doses—6:30 and 10:30. Then I just felt… out of it. Nauseous too, but that’s gone now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We did a CT scan of your head and abdomen—both came back normal. No bleeding, no stroke, no internal issues. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why the confusion? Is it the painkillers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very likely. Percocet contains an opioid, and in higher doses or with frequent use, especially with kidney issues, it can build up and cause drowsiness, confusion, nausea—exactly what you had.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… I didn’t know that. My kidney function isn’t great, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. Your baseline creatinine is around 1.4–1.9, and today it was 1.8—stable. But your kidneys clear medications more slowly, so opioids like Percocet can linger and affect you more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. So what now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve stopped the Percocet. Your mental status is already improving—you’re more alert. We’ll manage your pain with something safer for your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my arm? It still hurts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you a dose of ketorolac earlier, but we can’t use that long-term because of your kidney function. So we’re switching to Vicodin—also has an opioid, but we’ll use it carefully, only as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s similar, but we’ll limit how much you take and monitor you. And you and your wife should watch for drowsiness or confusion—if that happens, stop it and call your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about my heart and blood pressure meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on warfarin for your heart clot risk, and your INR was 3.0—perfect range. We continued amiodarone and metoprolol for your heart rhythm and function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been on those a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We also restarted lisinopril today—your blood pressure is stable, and we want to protect your heart. But we held spironolactone because your potassium was a bit high—5.2.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, right. I remember that from last time. So no spironolactone now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not for now. We’ll check your potassium again before restarting it. Your kidney function is stable—creatinine went from 1.8 to 2.0, which is expected and not concerning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my breathing? I’ve been a bit short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows mild fluid buildup in the lungs—common with heart failure. We’re keeping you on torsemide to help with that. You’re on oxygen now, but only 2 liters—we’ll wean that as you improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve had that before. What about the chest pain I had last week?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your troponin was normal, and EKG shows atrial fibrillation with mild changes, but no sign of a heart attack. The chest discomfort may have been from strain or your esophagus—it’s been an issue before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I have that dysmotility. So not my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unlikely. We’ll keep monitoring. You’re on telemetry, and your rhythm is stable AF at around 96—well controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are back. Blood and urine cultures show no infection. Tox screen was negative except for acetaminophen—which makes sense from the Percocet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no infection causing the confusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. And your thyroid, B12, and folate are normal—so not a metabolic or deficiency issue. Everything points to the Percocet as the cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much clearer today. Glad it wasn’t something worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and your potassium is down to 4.9—back to normal. We’ll keep monitoring your kidney function and restart lisinopril safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow. Your mental status is back to baseline, pain is manageable, and labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What meds am I going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue most of your usual meds: amiodarone, metoprolol, warfarin, torsemide, and lisinopril. We stopped Percocet and spironolactone. You’ll go home with Vicodin for pain—only as needed, one every four hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel foggy again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stop the Vicodin and call your doctor. Also, weigh yourself daily—call if you gain more than three pounds, which could mean fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. See your primary doctor within four days. Get your INR and basic blood work—Chem 7—done on the 6th, and send the results to him. You also have pulmonology and cardiology appointments soon—keep those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge. You’re alert, walking well, and your labs are stable. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I understand. Stop Vicodin if I feel off, watch my weight, see my doctor, get labs done. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And keep working on quitting smoking—we talked about that too. Take care, Mr. Johnson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.
